name: Arop-Lokep
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Raymond, Mary. 2006. Stress and syllabification in Arop-Lokep: an Optimality-Theoretic account. SOAS Working Papers in Linguistics 14: 109-129. (Secondary: D'Jernes, Lucille S. 2002. Arop-Lokep. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages, 249-269. Richmond: Curzon.)
catalog_locator: Raymond 2006 p. 111, sec. 2 'Default stress placement'; p. 109 Introduction; p. 127 sec. 7 'Summary of Arop-Lokep stress in OT'; exceptions pp. 113-114 and p. 117. D'Jernes 2002 pp. 249-250 sec. 1.2 'Phonotactics and stress' (IA).
catalog_quote: All major class lexical items must be stressed in Arop-Lokep. A stressed syllable is characterized by an increase in vowel duration and intensity. High pitch may be, but is not necessarily, a correlate of stress. By default, primary [ˈ] stress falls on the penultimate syllable of multi-syllabic words, with secondary stresses [ˌ] occurring on every second syllable to the left. Syllables closed with a coda consonant (VC, CVC) are “heavy” and must also be stressed. [p. 111] ... The phonological foot in Arop-Lokep is the moraic trochee. Stress is assigned from the right, with primary stress on the penultimate syllable. The language is unusual, however, in permitting secondary stress to the right of the main stress if the final syllable (which is not permitted to carry primary stress) is heavy, even if this creates a degenerate main foot in the penultimate position. This suggests that syllable weight is only relevant for secondary stress assignment and that other principles apply for the placement of primary stress. [p. 109] ... Firstly, it is a quantity-sensitive language; the WSP constraint is virtually unviolated. At the same time, however, primary stress nearly always falls on the penultimate syllable, even when this is a light syllable and the ultima is heavy. ... What these facts demonstrate is that while syllable weight is significant for the assignment of secondary stress, it is practically irrelevant for primary stress assignment. [p. 127]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words regardless of weight (a light penult keeps primary stress even before a heavy ultima); secondary stresses fall on every second syllable to the left, and every closed syllable must carry at least secondary stress, so a heavy final syllable is secondarily stressed to the right of the primary (e.g. [ˈmaˌtuk] 'coconut'; D'Jernes 2002 p. 250 hears this same word as final-stressed [ma.'tuk], i.e. as a heavy syllable attracting stress in disyllables). Foot = moraic trochee; monosyllables are stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: every second syllable to the left of the primary, plus obligatory (secondary) stress on every heavy (closed) syllable, including a word-final one to the right of the main stress (Raymond 2006 pp. 111-112; the Weight-to-Stress Principle is 'virtually unviolated', p. 127). Degenerate (single light) feet are tolerated to avoid lapse.
new_statements.exceptions: Subject-agreement prefixes on verbs are extrametrical: monosyllabic verb roots get primary stress on the ultima ([aˈpa] '1s+plant'), creating stress minimal pairs between verbs and nouns (pp. 113-114); 1pEXCL prefix am- is never stressed except before geminate-initial roots (pp. 114-115); some object-marking suffixes and lexical reduplication yield final primary stress or unparsed syllables (secs. 4-5, pp. 116-124); (C)VViCVi syllabification interacts with stress (sec. 6). D'Jernes 2002 (pp. 249-250) instead states that in disyllables heavy CVC/CVV syllables attract the stress away from the penult ([ma.'tuk], [be.'lei], [ka.'pok]), so the two descriptions disagree on whether the final heavy syllable carries primary or secondary stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, Arop dialect (Long Island, Madang Province); forms elicited from one main native speaker in isolation and in the frame 'I said ___ again', judged by three SIL linguists with Speech Analyzer waveform/intensity checks; stress cue = loudness + vowel duration, pitch unreliable (p. 110). The [ˈ] and [ˌ] in the quote are IPA stress marks whose glyphs lack a Unicode map in the PDF text (extracted text yields control characters); they are supplied from context ('primary [ˈ] stress', 'secondary stresses [ˌ]').
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe the Arop dialect (Long Island, Madang Province) of Arop-Lokep [apr]; the Lokep dialect (Tolokiwa Island, Masele on Umboi; also called Lokewe/Lukep) is only occasionally marked '(L)' in D'Jernes 2002 and one Lokep speaker's recordings were consulted for doubtful cases in Raymond 2006. Glottolog's languoid page as downloaded showed no separate dialect codes; none assigned here.

sources.note: Whole paper is on word stress (Arop dialect, one main consultant, perceptual + Speech Analyzer checks): stress predictable/non-contrastive apart from morphologically explicable cases; primary stress on the penult of polysyllables, secondary on every second syllable leftward; every closed (heavy) syllable must be stressed, so a heavy ultima gets secondary stress to the right of the primary; moraic trochee; extrametrical subject prefixes, object suffixes and reduplication produce exceptions incl. final primary stress on monosyllabic verb roots (pp. 109-129).

tone.quote: Stress in Arop-Lokep is predictable in the majority of cases, and is therefore not contrastive (with a few exceptions which can be accounted for on morphological grounds); therefore it need not be represented in the orthography. A stressed syllable is characterized by an increase in vowel duration and intensity. High pitch may be, but is not necessarily, a correlate of stress.
tone.summary: Full SIL phonology with no tone analysis; pitch mentioned only as a possible stress correlate. No explicit 'no tone' statement, so tone is left open rather than coded absent.
